title: Salience Network

html:
The salience network (SN) is a large-scale paralimbic-limbic system whose cortical anchors are the anterior insula/fronto-operculum and the dorsal/anterior mid-cingulate cortex, with a robust and often right-lateralized emphasis, especially in the anterior insula 1, 2, 3, 4. Subcortical affiliates are reliable and behaviorally interpretable: amygdala and ventral striatum (valuation and action vigor), mediodorsal thalamus and related thalamic relays, and arousal nuclei in the brainstem (notably the locus coeruleus and neighboring neuromodulatory complexes) that couple interoceptive state to whole-brain gain control 1, 5, 6, 7. Functionally, the SN performs rapid context appraisal and relevance signaling and, via the right anterior insula in particular, initiates network-level switches that up-regulate frontoparietal control while suppressing default-mode activity when salient events demand action 8, 9. This circuitry is closely allied with-but separable from-the cingulo-opercular (CON) "set-maintenance" network: across datasets, CON tracks tonic alertness and stable task set over extended epochs, whereas SN is optimized for detecting change and triggering mode shifts, together forming a complementary controller axis centered on insula-cingulate hubs 10, 11, 12. A 2026 human intracranial study maps four insular regions and an asymmetric anterior-to-posterior influence (Figure) 53. Insular regions link bodily signals with shifts in salience and action mode (Figure).

The salience network’s distinctive contribution is to govern state transitions between internally focused cognition and externally oriented control. In the "triple-network" framework, SN activity-centered on anterior insula and anterior/mid-cingulate-detects behaviorally relevant change and biases large-scale dynamics away from default-mode processing and toward frontoparietal and dorsal-attention engagement. Convergent evidence supports this switching role: fMRI effective-connectivity shows the right anterior insula exerting causal influence that suppresses DMN while recruiting executive circuitry; replications with dynamic causal modeling recover the same SN->DMN and SN->CEN directions; and intracranial electrophysiology reveals that task-evoked high-frequency activity peaks earlier in attention/control networks than in the DMN, with the SN’s response timing intermediate and consistent with an initiating role 8, 13, 14, 15. Mechanistically, anterior insula and cingulate signals ramp at salience detection and error, propagate to dorsolateral/frontoparietal nodes, and are accompanied by deactivation in core DMN hubs; perturbation and stimulation studies add causal weight by showing that modulating anterior insula alters conflict handling and attention reallocations 16, 15, 17. In the absence of salient external demands, SN drive relaxes and the DMN reasserts its baseline dominance for self-referential/internal mentation, consistent with longstanding observations of DMN activity at rest and its anticorrelation with task-positive systems 18, 19. Taken together, the SN orchestrates a context-appropriate balance-dampening introspective modes when action is required and releasing them when the environment permits-so that the agent pivots efficiently between internal simulation and outward, goal-directed control.

Salience computation begins with what these cortical hubs are built to represent. The posterior dorsal insula is the brain’s primary interoceptive sensory cortex: it receives high-fidelity thalamic relay of lamina-I signals for pain, temperature and visceral state, and its activity tracks graded pain intensity during sustained noxious stimulation 20, 21, 22. From there, information is relayed forward into dysgranular/anterior agranular insula where interoceptive maps are merged with exteroceptive and motivational context-taste and oral somatosensation in the mid/anterior insula, vestibular and motion cues in posterior/mid insula, and limbic value signals via dense amygdala and striatal connectivity 22, 23. This posterior->anterior gradient equips the anterior insula with a multimodal "state estimator" that can represent risk, surprise, and decision uncertainty (e.g., risk-prediction errors that update within a trial 24), rather than just raw bodily input 25. Microstructurally, the agranular fronto-insular cortex and dorsal ACC are enriched in large von Economo "spindle" neurons-thought to support rapid long-range broadcast-positioning these nodes to issue fast "global relevance" updates that bias processing elsewhere 26.

On the cingulate side, the dorsal ACC/mid-cingulate carries precisely the computations needed to turn those relevance estimates into control. Single-unit and imaging work shows that dACC neurons encode response conflict 27, learned error likelihood 28, prospective foraging value 29, and the cost-benefit "expected value of control," 30 consistent with a role in deciding when control is worth paying for and of what kind. Anatomically, dACC nests cingulate motor zones with outputs to premotor/M1 and even spinal targets, and it couples tightly to autonomic effectors; this lets relevance signals translate into immediate adjustments of attention, sampling, arousal, and action. In concrete terms, when the anterior insula infers a high-precision deviation-say, a sudden siren while driving-dACC can hike control demand and prepare skeletomotor and autonomic responses in the next beat 31, 32.

Computationally this division of labor fits predictive-coding accounts in which attention is the tuning of "precision," i.e., synaptic gain on prediction-error units 33, 34, 35. The anterior insula carries precision-weighted surprise signals in multiple domains (pain, value, risk) and sits at the apex of a network that can up-gain sensory and control circuits while down-regulating distractors 36; neuromodulatory coupling to the locus-coeruleus/noradrenergic system provides a plausible fast channel for these gain shifts during salience hits 37. Put together, the insula-dACC axis implements a relevance->control transform: insula computes that an event matters (because it perturbs the organism’s predicted internal/external state with high precision), and dACC decides and implements the control policy to handle it. Seen alongside the other control networks, the salience network (SN) is best characterized as a supervisor of when and where control is needed, rather than a system that represents what the current rules or contents are. The multiple-demand/frontoparietal network (FPN/MD) carries the parametric, content-specific representations that implement task rules and working memory, whereas the SN monitors the unfolding environment and internal state to decide if control should be intensified, relaxed, or reallocated. In contrast to the dorsal attention network (DAN; IPS/FEF), which maintains a continuous, top-down spatial priority map and selection policy, the SN is phasic and event-driven: it flags unexpected or urgent changes and biases DAN to "point the spotlight" and FPN to update or switch the active policy. Within SN, the dACC/aMCC implements the cost-benefit calculus for deploying control-coding conflict, error likelihood, and the expected value of control-providing a principled trigger for upshifts in top-down regulation when the payoff outweighs the effort. The anterior insula supplies the complementary "why it matters" signal: by integrating interoceptive/body-state cues with exteroceptive and affective value, it confers urgency and motivational significance on candidate events and helps initiate large-scale switches, especially from its right fronto-insular sector. Overall, a purely frontoparietal controller can execute a chosen rule set, but the SN biases whether to persist, escalate, or abandon that set in light of pain, threat, reward opportunity, uncertainty, or conflict-functionally operating as a high-level action selector that modulates DAN and FPN according to a holistic relevance assessment.

The centrality of the salience network (SN) shows up most starkly when it breaks. Because the SN sits high in the control hierarchy-as a gatekeeper for when to engage top-down systems-its disruption propagates through cognition. In schizophrenia, the classic "aberrant salience" account links dysregulated mesostriatal dopamine to misassignment of significance, with downstream insula-cingulate dysfunction producing unstable belief updating and the intrusion of internally generated content as externally meaningful; structural and functional evidence implicates anterior insula and dACC within the SN as core loci of this failure mode 38, 39, 40, 41. Anxiety and PTSD show the complementary problem: lowered thresholds in SN hubs yield hypervigilant, threat-biased appraisal, with anterior insula and dACC over-engagement, stronger stress-sensitive SN coupling, and difficulty disengaging once aroused 42, 43, 44. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Disorders marked by switching failures further reveal the SN’s role as a mode selector. In ADHD, deficits cluster around poor attenuation of the default-mode network (DMN) during task engagement and impaired cross-network coordination, consistent with an SN that fails to efficiently flip the system from internal mentation to externally driven control 45, 46, 47. Major depression shows a different imbalance-hyperconnected DMN with weakened SN coupling and perturbed insula-anchored interactions-which tracks rumination and blunted reactivity to behaviorally relevant change; effective-connectivity work and meta-analysis converge on this triple-network signature 48, 49, 50. Finally, degeneration of the very neurons that likely enable the SN’s rapid, broadcast control-von Economo and related fork cells in fronto-insular and cingulate cortex-produces the apathy, inertia, and loss of initiative that headline early behavioral-variant frontotemporal dementia, a clinicopathologic demonstration that when the SN’s motivational monitor goes offline, goal-directed behavior collapses 51, 52. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

In summary, the salience network provides an indispensable layer of control that complements other brain systems. It detects what matters most at each instant and tilts the entire cognitive apparatus accordingly - toggling between world-model introspection and environment interaction, mobilizing effort when needed and recovering idle mode when possible, and infusing executive commands with affective and interoceptive context.
